title: Discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities in real-world software with Claude
content:
Over the past few months, we’ve used an unreleased, internal research model to find critical vulnerabilities in some of the world’s most widely used software, such as browsers and operating systems. In this post, we share details of five attack chains, which led to remote code execution and other critical impacts with little to no user interaction. These attack chains demonstrate the model’s ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software. Any vulnerabilities in these products could affect billions of users. They’re also among the most security-critical software in the world, making them a bellwether for testing models’ vulnerability research and cyber capabilities.
We reported each vulnerability to the affected vendor under our coordinated vulnerability disclosure, which gives developers 90 days to patch and a further 45 days before we discuss details beyond what is already included in a public advisory.
1. One-click remote code execution in Chrome
After initial prompting, Claude wrote a full exploit chain enabling an attacker to execute arbitrary code as the user, outside the browser’s sandbox. Our proof of concept launches the Calculator app from a stock default-configuration Chrome browser on macOS within seconds of the page loading, without any further user interaction:
- Claude discovered a vulnerability in Chrome’s JavaScript engine, V8, that allowed a malicious web page to corrupt V8’s heap memory.
- Claude discovered a second vulnerability to break out of V8’s memory region sandbox and defeat ASLR. This step located Chrome’s code in memory and used a return-oriented programming (ROP) chain to take full control of the renderer process.
- The compromised renderer was confined by Chrome’s process sandbox. Claude then discovered a race condition in CacheStorage. The compromised renderer used the race condition to read memory outside the sandbox and learn the memory layout of the privileged browser process.
- Finally, Claude discovered a use-after-free in FedCM, Chrome’s federated sign-in feature, that allowed the exploit to execute arbitrary code outside the sandbox.
We have reported our findings to Google: 62 CVEs have been assigned and patched as of Chrome 156, with all of them rated critical or high severity. Among them are 13 sandbox escapes and 21 vulnerabilities that could have been used to compromise the renderer.
2. A one-click exploit chain in Safari
After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit chain that let any website’s JavaScript completely bypass the same-origin policy (SOP). The exploit could access a user’s Safari history, cookies, and other sensitive data, and could send authenticated HTTP requests to other domains and read the responses. For example, if the user is signed in to their email account, the attacker can now read their email; if they’re logged into their bank account, the attacker can view account balances or attempt transfers.
To do this, Claude defeated several layers of protection built into Safari:
- Claude discovered a use-after-free (UAF) vulnerability in JavaScriptCore, Safari’s JavaScript engine, which is written in C++. Certain TypedArray operations wrote through stale pointers to freed memory, overwriting TypedArray metadata.
- WebKit’s Gigacage mitigates this type of attack by isolating TypedArray data in a separate region of memory. Claude discovered that certain variables in this region were used to index into other regions, which gave it an arbitrary read/write primitive outside the Gigacage.
- All website JavaScript runs in the WebContent sandbox, which keeps bugs like the UAF from reaching sensitive browser data on disk. Claude discovered a vulnerability in the sandbox's IPC mechanism that let the exploit read Safari’s stored history, cookies, and session databases from disk.
- Finally, Claude used the UAF to overwrite a variable in memory and disable the SOP, allowing the attacker’s page to read data from any other origin.
The chain is interesting because it is a data-only attack that never relies on arbitrary code execution. Instead, it uses full read/write access to the browser process’s memory to modify a security flag, an object size, and a URL. Several of the weaknesses are not vulnerabilities on their own but intended behaviors that become exploitable when combined.
Apple acknowledged our report the same day we submitted it and implemented a fix promptly. That fix is available to users.
3. Android lock screen bypass
After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit that let an attacker extract photos and other personal information from a stolen Android phone without unlocking it. The work combined three methods: source code analysis of the open-source parts of Android, reverse engineering and deobfuscation of the Google Play services binaries, and live testing on a physical Google Pixel 9. This turned up a wide range of vulnerabilities in both the open-source and proprietary components. Claude then chained three of them into the final exploit.
Android has several layers of protection against this attack. Claude found a way around each one:
- A locked Android phone is designed not to transfer data over USB. Claude found that a USB host with a specific setting bypassed this.
- The device-to-device transfer protocol refuses data commands from unauthorized peers. Claude found a way to skip the authorization check and start the pairing process.
- Pairing is protected by an authenticated key agreement that asks the user to verify a six-digit code. Claude found a flaw that skipped this verification and behaved as if the user had tapped “Allow.”
- USB transfers are not supposed to carry file contents, as enforced by a hardcoded check. Claude found a fallback mechanism that sent raw bytes over USB and was not covered by the check. The exploit requested file contents through it.
This issue has been addressed by Google.
4. Windows remote denial of service
After initial prompting, Claude wrote an exploit that would have allowed an attacker to remotely crash any Windows machine that responds to HTTP/3 requests using the native Windows implementation. The difficulty in this case was in identifying the vulnerability in the first place. Following that initial prompting, we reported this vulnerability directly to Microsoft, which resolved the vulnerability and assigned it CVE-2026-33096.
The vulnerability that Claude identified was a memory safety out-of-bounds read in the Windows kernel’s implementation of QUIC. An attacker could reach the vulnerable codepath remotely over the network and send a few packets of data to a listening server to crash and restart the machine. By repeatedly sending these requests, it is possible to continuously crash the server, which causes loss of access to the server for all of the users. We estimate that there are likely several million such servers listening on the internet.
Claude discovered this vulnerability through binary analysis. We provided the model with a copy of the Windows executable and asked Claude to reverse-engineer how the software works using the existing reverse-engineering tools (such as Ghidra), write a fully annotated C program that reproduces the relevant features, compare the behavior reproduced program to binary to ensure correctness, and then study the code for vulnerabilities. When we asked Claude to identify potentially higher-risk issues, it surfaced this remotely exploitable vulnerability.
5. Zero-click remote code execution in Linux
While this post focuses on third-party products, our work on open source has continued. With Claude, we discovered local privilege escalation vulnerabilities on OpenBSD, FreeBSD, and Linux; a number of sandbox escapes in popular sandboxing infrastructure; and numerous vulnerabilities in important web applications. We have also found remotely triggerable (zero-click) arbitrary code execution vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel’s networking stack, which have since been

report.summary: Anthropic's internal Claude model autonomously found and chained critical zero-day exploits in Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows and Linux, producing dozens of patched CVEs.
report.background: Frontier labs have spent the past two years pushing AI models into vulnerability research, from DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge to Google's Big Sleep and a wave of startup bug-hunting agents. Most early results were single memory-safety bugs in fuzzed open-source code. This work goes further: multi-step exploit chains against hardened, heavily audited targets. Browsers and OS kernels are the bellwether because they combine sandboxing, ASLR, memory isolation and years of adversarial fuzzing with billions of affected users. Anthropic used an unreleased internal research model, not a public product, and followed coordinated disclosure: 90 days to patch, plus 45 before publishing details.
key_points: Chrome one-click remote code execution: Claude chained four separate bugs, a V8 heap-corruption flaw, a second bug to defeat the V8 sandbox and ASLR with a ROP chain, a CacheStorage race condition leaking the privileged browser process's memory layout, and a FedCM use-after-free escaping the sandbox entirely. Google assigned and patched 62 CVEs by Chrome 156, including 13 sandbox escapes.

Safari same-origin-policy bypass: Claude built a data-only attack with no code execution. It used a use-after-free in JavaScriptCore's TypedArray handling, escaped WebKit's Gigacage memory isolation, exploited an IPC flaw in the WebContent sandbox to read Safari's history and cookies from disk, then overwrote a flag to disable the same-origin policy. Apple fixed it quickly.

Android lock-screen bypass: Claude combined AOSP source review, reverse engineering of obfuscated Google Play services binaries, and live testing on a Pixel 9. It bypassed the USB data-transfer block, skipped device-pairing authorization, faked the six-digit verification tap, and used an unchecked fallback path to pull raw file bytes from a locked phone. Google patched it.

Windows HTTP/3 denial of service: using Ghidra-assisted binary reverse engineering, Claude reconstructed the Windows kernel QUIC implementation as annotated C, compared behavior against the binary, and found an out-of-bounds read reachable with a few packets. Repeatedly crashing potentially millions of internet-facing servers. Microsoft fixed it as CVE-2026-33096.

Open-source breadth: Beyond third-party products, the model found local privilege-escalation bugs in OpenBSD, FreeBSD and Linux, multiple sandbox escapes in common sandboxing infrastructure, flaws in major web applications, and zero-click remote code execution in the Linux kernel's networking stack, showing the capability generalizes across targets.
report.impact: The key shift is economic: exploit development, historically gated by scarce human expertise and months of work, is becoming cheap and automatable. Defenders now face a world where bug discovery outpaces patch deployment, and where chained, non-obvious flaws (intended behaviors combined into exploits) are exactly what models are good at finding. For developers, the practical lesson is to assume adversarial code review at machine scale and to prioritize sandbox boundaries, IPC surfaces and memory-safe rewrites. For users, expect faster patches but also shorter windows between disclosure and exploitation. Policy questions around disclosure timelines, dual-use model access and licensing for security research will intensify.
report.tools: Follow Ghidra and Binary Ninja for reverse engineering, AFL++ and libFuzzer for fuzzing, AddressSanitizer and OSS-Fuzz for memory-safety testing. For AI-driven research, watch Google Project Zero's Big Sleep, Anthropic's coordinated-disclosure posts, and CVE/NVD advisories for Chrome, WebKit and the Linux kernel. Claude itself (API or Claude Code) is usable for assisted code and binary analysis under responsible-disclosure rules.
